Messages.Author: Mark Allen
Messages.Body:
We had our storyline today. I was very suprised to be the victim of what I
would call a slight oversight on the creators of The Archon. We had 5
players and I was player '2'. When the 3rd round occured, I was completely
stunned to discover that I was first, again. Checking the Optimal Seating
page in the Archon spreadsheet, we found the following:

5 Players
Round 1 1 2 3 4 5
Round 2 2 5 3 1 4
Round 3 2 1 5 4 3

Now, I don't mind being first but when there are 3 other Meths that haven't
been first by the end of the 3rd round, I find this just wrong. I suggest
this should be changed or reviewed. If there is a reason why the seating
exists so that the 2nd player starts first for two rounds, I would like to
hear it. For the 3rd round, I suggest the following:

5,4,3,2,1 OR 4,3,2,1,5 OR 3,2,1,5,4

This would 'spread out' the players that are first and still not cause a
seating arrangement so that the there are players with the same
prey/predator relationship for different rounds.

Anyone have comments on this? Am I just crazy?

Mark Allen
Prince of Ottawa

I'll dispute that 5th seat is the worst.

I often like going 5th if I'm playing a fast bleed deck. With 4
transfers, Info Highway, Dreams and Zillah's available, it quite
possible to influence out a vampire on your first turn. Your prey will
likely have only had 5 transfers so they are potentially stuck eating
your first bleed with no defense, if not your predator's first bleed
(via bounce) as well! This can give you the Edge which often doesn't
move during the second turn--Meths are wary of intercept since minions
are usually in play, and no one wants their first vampire torpored
with no chance to rescue.

The major drawbacks to going 5th aren't really that bad IMO. You don't
get any "extra" transfers. The main problem is with contestation of
Master cards, but that doesn't happen that often right out of the gate
in my experience.

As you might have seen in the thread LSJ linked to, I did end
up agreeing that while seats 1-4 are (with the caveat that
for a particular deck you have in mind, this may not be true)
equally good/bad. Seat 5 is worse because you have to go
later than player #4 without getting any more transfers in
exchange for going later.

That is, going first is supposed to be just as good as going
second, because while you only get 1 transfer on your first
turn, you get to play a master card and discard a card before
they get a turn, and on your second turn you can act before
them if you have a 1-capacity vampire, etc. Going fifth,
though, your predator gets as many transfers, master phases,
and discards as you do on their first turn, *and* they'll
get to take an action with those transfers before you do.

Now, for any specific deck, it might be that going first is
worse than going fourth (or even fifth!) because all of your
vampires are 8-caps or something, and you don't have any
early-game masters to get some use out of taking an earlier
turn than the fourth- and fifth-seat players. But when
developing seating charts, the only assumption we can make
about the players' decks is that they will have at least 12
vampires in their crypts and 60 cards in their libraries.
:-) In other words, we assume that for the entire population
of possible VTES decks, going first is a good thing for about
as many decks as it's a bad thing for.

> As I say I would generally rather repeat 5th than 1st. I don't think
> I've ever heard anyone groan at being 5th whereas I regularly hear
> groans over being first.

This turns out to be mainly because people don't realize
that they're getting screwed by being 5th, I think. :-)
They're happy to get out a vampire on "their" first or
second turn, without considering that their predator got
to have just as many transfers, got to take his/her turn
earlier, and had a predator with fewer transfers.

Josh

Do you know of an algorithm that will determine a worthwhile VTES
deck, then? Could you post it please, it will make deck designing a
whole lot simpler.

> As you rightly pointed out to LSJ, while the discard
> is potentially useful, you are unlikely to know
> what you should discard.

I don't know about that. In the first round of a tournament you may
not know anything about your opponents' decks, but in subsequent
rounds you may know enough to determine whether certain cards are
useful or not. Even apart from that you should always be able to look
at your hand in isolation and decide *if* something needs to be
discarded, some cards are only really handy later (foreshadowing
destruction, for example), others are only useful with other cards
(ghouled, for example), and you hardly ever want your hand full of
something (votes, for example). True, you may not always want to use
your discard as first player- but if you do, which I find is quite
common for highly focused decks, then it is very useful indeed.

> I reckon that the disadvantage 5 has to 4 is much smaller than the
> advantage 5 has over 1 -I'd take a small disadvantage to my predator for
> a bigger one over my prey.

How does 5 have an advantage over 1? By the time 5's first minion
gets to act, 1 has already had an opportunity to act, has had one more
transfer and has had the same number of master phases and one more
discard.

> Consider the capacity point you can get out:
>
> Round/Player

> 1 1 2 3 4 4
> 2 5 6 7 8 8
> 3 9 10 11 12 12

> you will be better off with the 6cap -which
> puts you at a disadvantage when you sit in
> place 1.

You are assuming all transfers go onto a single vampire and that a
larger capacity vampire is better than a smaller. Neither assumption
is always true.

LSJ,

When checking for a repeated seating order, should "cross-table" in a
4 player game be considered the same thing as "grand-prey/predator" in
a 5 player? I.e. if in round 1 I (A) am cross-table from another
player (B), on a four-player table, should this prevent A X B and B X
A seatings on subsequent five-player tables?

* lehrbuch

Looking at the size of this thread and the fact that for every argument in
one direction, there seems to be a 'solid' argument in the opposite, it
brings me to one conclusion: there isn't a huge difference where you start,
and even if there was, sometimes you get some good luck - sometimes bad. The
hand and crypt that you start with (IMHO) are significantly more important
than if you get 1, 2...4 transfers in the first turn. It is a game that is a
combination of luck and strategy. Concentrate on those variables that you
can affect, and cross your fingers (or use whatever method of improving your
luck you choose) for those you can't.

A previous thread pointed out that solving this sort of problem, with so
many variables and so many starting conditions is at the very best,
non-trivial, and is very likely to be intractable. I for one think that the
seating arrangements are fine as they are. As long as there are no glaringly
obvious errors (ie. violations of the first couple of seating 'rules'),
which I suspect would have been pointed out and corrected by now, then go
with the luck of the draw and good luck to you all!

If you think you have a better way, then propose that method, and let others
peer review your work. Simply pointing the finger and saying "it's broke,
you made it like that, you fix it" is exactly the sort of problem that I see
regularly in SO many places. It is better to approach a problem with "I
believe that this isn't as good as it could be. Do you mind if I have a go a
proposing a better system?" is a MUCH better methodology.

Also, the continual back and forth of "I disagree - here's an example" is
simply one-upmanship and manages to prove nothing. There have also been some
claims of 'proof' that have been based upon incorrect math. Unless you know
statistics very well, it is easy to get it very wrong, especially when
basing it upon what intuitively appears to be correct. (I am not going to
point fingers, because it doesn't matter in the slightest to the outcome of
the 'argument'.) Instead, I will again say, if you have a better system,
propose it and let us look at it in the same light as you looked at the
current system - if not, belt up and find something else to think about.

Try to enjoy the game, not get embroiled in the minutiae! (Except for LSJ,
of course, being that it's his job!)

Cheers all!

If I've read Peter Bakija correctly (and please, somebody correct
me if I'm wrong), the theory behind pounding every minion that your
prey brings out as quickly as she brings them out is this: If you
keep killing their minions, they'll have to keep bringing out more,
thereby draining their pool. This should be much faster than bleeding
for one and occasionally torporizing bouncers or blockers.

Personally, I agree that it's much better to wait and just do little
bleeds until your prey is almost ready to oust your grandprey, or shortly
before that (I tend to err on the side of caution, when I remember to).
The time you spend defending, by shredding enough of your predator's
minions to make her clam up, will act as enough psychological deterrent
to your prey to keep them from messing with you, encourage them to race
to kill your grandprey, or both. Whenever I tried just killing my prey's
guys to get at their pool by making them bring out more guys, I almost
always ended up with not enough cards left in my deck to really do much
after my prey was ousted.

Kushiel

I think this depends on what your ousting strategy is. If you're
packing Fame/TitR, I'd focus on knocking down my predator's minions to
keep him off my back because I'm probably playing less pool management
(to make room for the Fames/TitR). If I was using bleeds, I'd knock
down my prey's vampires first to keep them from generating pool and
force him to spend down his pool to keep playing the game. In either
situation you'll likely have to rush both ways, but that's how I
determine my priorities.

It's very important that as a combat deck player you size up the table
balance quickly. If you knock down your predator's blockers when your
grand-predator is a S/B deck, you're drastically unbalancing the
table. On the other hand, beating up your prey will lead to the
aforementioned strong grand-prey problem or a walled-up prey that will
be tough to oust in time. You need to be able to see who is near an
oust and how that will influence the game since you need not only your
prey's VP, but also 1 other in order to win by being the last player
standing.

The judge will randomly assign players in groups of five. In the event

groups as possible contain five players.

randomizing method.

Correct. I think the whole idea of playing slow is very
counterproductive to what a Ruch deck does.

You hit the ground running. Kill every vampire your prey brings out as
quickly as possible. If they bring out more vampires, you kill them
too, costing them more pool, allowing you to oust them faster. If they
don't bring out more vampires, you can just bleed them out at your
leisure, rushing defensively as necessary, as they aren't going to be
gaining more pool at any significant rate. Kill them quickly. If you
give them time to set up, your attacks get foiled, they gain more
pool, whatever.

Just hit the ground running and kill, kill, kill, kill, kill the poor.

The rush deck is all about killing your 1st prey as quickly as
possible, and then playing a waiting/defensive game till the game
comes down to you and one other guy, and you should be the last one
standing--Rush decks live and die by the 3 VPs necessary to get a
table win. Sometimes you can pull off 4. I've gotten 5 at least once
with a Rush deck. Usually, though, it is all about getting 3. To this
end, just tear into your prey as quickly and brutally as possible,
only Rushing up stream as necessary to stay alive. Once your prey is
dead and you have 1 VP, it is time to hunker down like a rabid hedge
hog and just stay alive.

Yeah, it isn't fun to be the prey of a good Rush deck--unless you have
reasonable combat defense (which isn't that hard to have, but it is
often ignored), you might not even get to take a single action. Yes,
it is a drag. But it is also a drag to get stealth bled for 15 in two
turns, and that happens far more often.

potentially foil you. If you kill every vampire he puts into play
before it takes an action, you have a much easier time ousting them.
More than once have I lost a game simply because for whatever reason
one of my prey's vampires survived till the turn after he came out
(hand jam, lucky combat defense, something) and got Minion Tapped,
meaning I had to bleed through another 6 or 8 pool, which isn't
insignificant.

Letting your prey get set up is just asking to lose. Kill. That is why
the deck exists.

> minions to make her clam up, will act as enough psychological deterrent
> to your prey to keep them from messing with you, encourage them to race
> to kill your grandprey, or both.

have a whole new, un-mangled, fresh and new predator with 6 more pool
than you. Rush forward with reckless abandon. Ruch backwards shrewedly
as needed. Don't rush cross table, ever. The only time I'll ever rush
cross table is when someone does something to cost me the from across
the table (like Kindred Restructures to steal my hard earned VP)--once
I have been tooled and I in a losing position due to crosstable

nowadays, I think, have come to find this philosophy
useful in that it helps avoid becoming the target of
table wrath too early in the game. Table wrath is bad.
:-)

There's also the argument that demolishing your prey
immediately seriously upsets table balance, in that your
grandprey gets pretty much a free hand for as long as it
takes you to oust your prey. If that's even a turn or
two too much, he may have 2 VPs by the time you get to
him, and be too far ahead of you to catch up - ie if you
can't then crush *him* instantly, he'll oust you before
you do.

None of this is to deny the potential effectiveness of
the "attack left until there ain't nothing left to attack"
approach. It can work. It can work well. But there are
other possible routes to victory, especially when/if an
area's table politics have come to a point where you have
to be subtle to not be preemptively stopped.

Josh

hard. Like gain more pool. Or recruit chump blockers. Or rescue
vampires from torpor. Or Sensory Deprive me. Or move the table around
so that he isn't my prey any more.

an action. Ever. 'Cause all of his vampires are dead. That way, you
get a quick VP, 6 more pool, and can then act to manage the table such
that you win. You might not, sure, but it is a good way to start to
try.

threads that erupt around the idea) from the "precognitive table
management" syndrome--rather than just killing your prey, people look
at the table early, and try to figureout what will happen in the

Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes
Messages.Body:
On 18 Sep 2003, Peter D Bakija wrote:

> Exactly. If your deck's main plan for winning the game is "kill
> people", then letting your prey set up in the name of "not looking too
> scary" is just asking to lose.

I disagree. At least, this isn't necessarily true. One of the
differences we're going to have in this discussion is that you're driving
a weenie deck, while I am driving a multi-rush deck. I'll even concede
that weenies are "better". But, it's not something I or many other people
are going to play, there are other deck styles that rely on rush, and
strategies that work for one don't necessarily work for the other.

Given the weenie focus, you have a lot of minion actions, but I think the
actual combat is pretty narrow. There are going to be a lot of things
that stymie you. It's more important for your deck to not let the prey
get a toe-hold than it would be for, say, Karsh, or Wynn, or
Lazernuts. These types of decks can be built in such a way that you can
be reasonably confident of mowing through whatever anti-combat they are
playing. In such a case, the benefits of them spending 15 pool outweigh
the risk that their deck actually gets to function. As with so many
weenie decks, half your deck's strength relies on denying the opponent the
ability to play his. More robust decks (while more fragile in other ways,
and probably overall) don't need to live in fear that their neighbors may
get to act.

> Yeah, if you pound them from the get
> go, the rest of the table might look at you and say "ooh. scary." and
> then gang up on you and kill you. But they also might not. On the
> other hand, if you let your prey set up, he *will* do everything he
> can to foil your killing, and it might just work.

Hopefully, he'll also take a stab at killing his prey. I get your point
about getting the first VP and then being free to wall up. What I don't
concede is that this particular deck you're discussing does particularly
well with "one forward, the rest back". IME, mono-potence just doesn't
kill things *that* well to survive successive and possibly
Darwinianly-selected predators smashing up against them.

Also consider this: a fast grab of one VP and turtling up *may*
work. Is it necessarily better than pinging your prey with light bleeds
while he comes close to ousting his prey, *then* dropping Fame and
multi-rushing him into the dirt, and grabbing a quick two n' twelve? Then
you turtle up with even more pool and fewer successive players to wall up
against. And you were never the table threat. Outside of leveraging the
weenie advantages of little pool expendatures and blah-blah-blah, even a
little extra "love" from across the table can spell disaster.

> If you build a deck to kill things, then kill them.

Yes, all in good time. As I think I mentioned, there may be tables where
you do just hurl yourself at your prey, and basically play it the way
you've described. But it wouldn't be my first choice, and espousing it as
the One True Way is poor advice to the people trying to learn this
game. Unless, perhaps, you also advise that they just play -- and only
play -- your deck. Even with that deck, though, I'd still hang back a
little and see what my prey will do.

> If my prey never takes an action, he can't do anything to make my life
> hard. Like gain more pool. Or recruit chump blockers. Or rescue
> vampires from torpor. Or Sensory Deprive me. Or move the table around
> so that he isn't my prey any more.

And, yet, these things aren't equivelant to "you lose". None of them are
good, and we'd rather not have impediments thrown in our way, but Rabid
Rush creates its own impediments that you are hand-waving away.

> The optimal situation for any Rush deck is when your prey never takes
> an action. Ever. 'Cause all of his vampires are dead. That way, you
> get a quick VP, 6 more pool, and can then act to manage the table such
> that you win. You might not, sure, but it is a good way to start to
> try.

But how do you get that "quick" 6 pool? Bleeding for one with your six
minions? Is your prey going to just keep bringing out minions? You say
yourself the goal is him not getting to play. If I'm clearly not going to
get to play no matter what I do, why should I stupidly feed into your
strategy, when you were the guy who just made me waste two hours of my
life in a non-game?

For a deck that can lunge, say via Freak Drive, I'd much rather let them
spend themselves down to around ten pool and then drop Fame on them,
followed by a couple of repeated dunk and rescues for the oust out of
nowhere.

Messages.Body:
David Cherryholmes wrote

> I disagree. At least, this isn't necessarily true. One of the
> differences we're going to have in this discussion is that you're driving
> a weenie deck, while I am driving a multi-rush deck.

Oh, absolutely. I coming completely from a weenie rush perspective. A
multi rush deck is going to be both more flexible and more capable of
picking up later if it lets its prey grow some, so it'll do better
this way. But then the multi rush deck has different weaknesses.

> I'll even concede
> that weenies are "better". But, it's not something I or many other people
> are going to play, there are other deck styles that rely on rush, and
> strategies that work for one don't necessarily work for the other.

Absolutely. Again, I am coming completely from the weenie rush
perspective.

> Hopefully, he'll also take a stab at killing his prey. I get your point
> about getting the first VP and then being free to wall up. What I don't
> concede is that this particular deck you're discussing does particularly
> well with "one forward, the rest back". IME, mono-potence just doesn't
> kill things *that* well to survive successive and possibly
> Darwinianly-selected predators smashing up against them.

It often depends on what you are faced with. Most of the game wins I
come up with, however, come from ousting my first pray quickly, and
then treading water/going backwards and forwards some till it comes
down to a 2 person game, and then winning from there. Going forward
constantly has its advantages too, depending on what is where.

> Also consider this: a fast grab of one VP and turtling up *may*
> work. Is it necessarily better than pinging your prey with light bleeds
> while he comes close to ousting his prey, *then* dropping Fame and
> multi-rushing him into the dirt, and grabbing a quick two n' twelve?

I'd say yes, as by then, he may have twice as much pool as he had
before due to Minion Taps. And he might have chump blockers to foil
rush attempts. And he might have defensive locations making rushing
difficult. And they might set up the vote network needed to rearrange
the table. If they never do anything (or close to it), they won't have
anything like this. It is usually *much* easier killing 1 minion a
turn for 3 or 4 turns than it is 3 or 4 minions in one turn.

> Yes, all in good time. As I think I mentioned, there may be tables where
> you do just hurl yourself at your prey, and basically play it the way
> you've described. But it wouldn't be my first choice, and espousing it as
> the One True Way is poor advice to the people trying to learn this
> game. Unless, perhaps, you also advise that they just play -- and only
> play -- your deck. Even with that deck, though, I'd still hang back a
> little and see what my prey will do.

Meh. I'm handing out the advice that makes the world go round--kill
your prey. Too much of this game is sullied by folks who don't realize
that killing your prey is what you are supposed to do. If I come
across a tad hyperbolically, then so be it. I'm willing to err on the
side of convincing people that killing their prey is always a good
idea. 'Cause it is.

Granted, if my prey brings out, say, a Gangrel as their first vampire,
I'll often hang back and see what he does. 'Cause if my prey is a
fortitude/protean Gangrel deck, I'm hosed. But if my prey brings out a
vampire with limited to no combat ability apparent, it is going down
right quick.

> But how do you get that "quick" 6 pool? Bleeding for one with your six
> minions? Is your prey going to just keep bringing out minions? You say
> yourself the goal is him not getting to play. If I'm clearly not going to
> get to play no matter what I do, why should I stupidly feed into your
> strategy, when you were the guy who just made me waste two hours of my
> life in a non-game?

If you keep bringing out minions, I kill them and you lose pool. If
you don't bring out minions, I bleed you for +/- 6 a turn while you
are gaining zero. And I might Fame the one you did bring out. Either
way works out fine. You start with 30. You bring out a 6 point minion
(nice and average). It dies before you get anything from it. You have
24 pool left. If you don't bring out any minions and spend any more
pool, you are going to be ousted in about 4 turns (multiple bleeds,
Computer Hackings, maybe some fame abuse), which, early in the game,
is pretty fast.

Yes. Sitting to the left of a rush deck, if you aren't packing
reasonable combat defense (Obediance, Fortitude, fight back--a good
handfull of Potence or Protean can totally *hose* a rush deck like
mad), sucks. You are just getting killed. But so does sitting next to
a Malk S+B deck if you aren't packing a dozen deflecitons. And you get
ousted just as fast.

> For a deck that can lunge, say via Freak Drive, I'd much rather let them
> spend themselves down to around ten pool and then drop Fame on them,
> followed by a couple of repeated dunk and rescues for the oust out of
> nowhere.

Which can certainly work. Especially in something like a Lasvernus
multi rush deck that has a lot more room for flexibility (like bounce
and Conditionings). But so can just hitting the ground running with a
weenie rush deck.

-Peter

Messages.Author: lehrbuch
Messages.Body:
pd...@lightlink.com (Peter D Bakija) wrote in message news:<aadbb36b.0309...@posting.google.com>...
> Correct. I think the whole idea of playing slow is very
> counterproductive to what a Ruch deck does.
>
> You hit the ground running. Kill every vampire your prey
> brings out as quickly as possible. If they bring out
> more vampires, you kill them too...

Absolutely. If you start letting your prey's minions get actions
before you know it they've all got leather jackets and .44s and the
zombies and war ghouls are out. Thumping fat vampires before they're
minion tapped is also vital.

The point of weenie combat is to get up and hitting quickly. Because
*your* vampires are small they are fragile and if your prey gets an
opportunity to get his defences organised you are screwed.

As Peter and others state this is totally different if you're playing
a fattie rush deck, In this case you will probably need to do some
equiping or something to protect your investment. At least
observation of your prey's disciplines is needed before you can go
careening willy nilly into combat. A protean surprise, for example,
isn't a critical error with rushing weenies, but it often is with
rushing fatties.

* lehrbuch

pd...@lightlink.com (Peter D Bakija) wrote in message news:<aadbb36b.03091...@posting.google.com>...
> David Cherryholmes wrote
> > Because your predator is really aggressive? I can't think of any good

> > reasons to auto-squish your prey, though.
>

> You win the game by ousting your prey. If you auto squish your prey,
> he doesn't get to generate more pool through actions or master card
> plays on that minion; he doesn't get to set up defensive technology;
> he doesn't get to move quick and oust his prey and gain 6 more pool.
>
> Kill your prey. That is how the game was designed. And how Rush decks
> work best. Just like most other decks.
>
> -Peter

I agree that you have to go after your prey, but like others have
said, it can also be counter-productive. I too am of the school of
"lie low, then lunge for the VP". I think the key point as you
acknowledged before is that this "kill, kill, then kill some more"
strategy only applies to weenie combat because it cannot deal with an
entrenched prey. A multi-rush or fattie-rush deck will be able to
counter the entrenched prey and cannot bleed as fast, so letting the
prey spend down his pool makes more sense. It all depends on the
combat deck you're playing, there is no One True Path to victory with
combat, but all roads do lead to your prey at some point.

Aramis
